title: 2026/09/03 - TI
machineSummary: The Infrastructure Commission says land transport unit costs tripled over two decades. Officials said a $7–$9 billion second harbour crossing requires tolls to fund renewals. Debates focused on limiting project scope, citing the City Rail Link, and funding the commission's new asset management assurance programs.

chunks.text: Morning, Jeff. You're on mute. How's that? That's great. I think, is Raveen joining us as well? I am-- He's, yeah, I think he's waiting to get in. Okay. Right. We'll wait till he's in, and then we'll get ourselves underway. Okay.
Morning, Paul.
Morning, Paul.

No, we don't have Raveen. Sure. I think. So nobody else is waiting? No. Jeff, Raveen's not waiting at the moment. So- They're saying that they can see you, but they have audio and video issues. I think maybe they need to... We have Shane Egan.
Yeah.

Will take us a moment to make sure we've got everybody online together. Yeah, I'll just give you an answer for this one. Okay. Yeah, sure. Yes, now. Jeff, can you hear us? Yes, I can. I can. Okay. Good. Just setting for video.
No, it's only until 9:00. Go to full doc. Go to the... Go to the business. That one? Yeah. Right.
Okay, we can see you now. Okay. I think it's just me though. Yeah, the same. Yeah. Maybe you should put it... Yeah, obviously.
Zoom is a wonderful thing when it's working. Yeah.

Right. Okay. Looks better. Nice to see you all there. Good morning. Good morning. Look, welcome. Thank you very much for this time, and I know we had to move it from last week because, I think it was illness and availability on your side. But welcome. I hope everybody's feeling good now.

And I think this, really, where we kicked this off from was, we've had the National Infrastructure Plan. We've had the government's response to that. Also, the opposition parties contributing to that, which is a good thing. But then you, we take-- This is really is about the next steps from there, and I think the opportunity for us to ask you some questions about where to from here, operationalizing that plan, and yeah, delivering a pipeline of infrastructure and delivering the right infrastructure in the right way. So, do you want to kick off, Raveen and Jeff, with any comments you want to

make, and then we'll go to questions? Not from me, Chair, because it's a very short one hour, so we'd rather use all the time taking your questions. Okay. And Jeff, you're fine as well? Yeah, I'm fine with that. Yeah. Okay. Well, look, colleagues, some questions. So who's going to kick us off? Tangy.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you all for joining us online. I guess the first one is just a top high-level question, and that is obviously the government have indicated their response to the plan. You've heard from other parties as well. What are some sort of top-level reactions from the commission without delving into the specific detail?

I think that will come through in the course of the meeting. Oh, yeah. Specific for the commission? Yes, please. Yeah. I think that there's probably- Probably... probably three that I would highlight. The first is associated with recommendation two. The minister has asked us to do some work looking at trying to better understand- Mm-hmm... the origin of cost escalation from the land transport sector.

Hang on, Jeff. Jeff, just hang on a moment. We're getting a lot of feedback, I presume, between the two. Yeah, course. There's an echo going on there. Quite a big echo. Someone needs to turn off their microphone. Yeah, I think there's a microphone turn off, I think, maybe for all of you in at the moment, and then we carry on. Sorry, Jeff.

Okay. Is that any better? Yeah. Yes. It is. Okay. Yeah. So point one is this work that we've been asked to now do associated with recommendation two in the National Infrastructure Plan, which is decomposing and understanding where the cost escalation in the land transport sector has come from. We released a sort of preliminary findings, well, not preliminary findings, but sort of casting a view over all of the work we've done looking at costs and infrastructure yesterday, and that gives you a bit of a flavor for how we

are thinking about this one. But one of the main points from that was looking at unit costs in land transport. We've seen those at or a little bit higher than tripling over the last decade or two. So there's a big question here about what is the origins of that. In large part because these things are spilling over into other areas of Crown investments. And, so that's why I think this has been a particularly large systemic issue.

The second one would probably be the recommendation there around assurance of both projects and the second part of this, of asset management assurance as well. The asset management assurance one really talks to the recommendations in the plan around looking after existing assets and getting on top of renewal cycles and so on. And the project-level assurance is very much about improving the front end, amongst other parts of planning for infrastructure, but getting a consistent process for how we assess infrastructure projects, and that is the adaptation

of gateway into the investment decision assurance program that the commission will be establishing from November 1. Thank you. Did you say there were three? Yeah. Well, I was bundling asset management assurance and project- Okay... assurance, which, yeah. Yep. The asset management assurance being something that is brand new, and we haven't done before.

So, that stands a little differently. In terms of the asset management assurance, given that it's new, some of the other stuff you have experience in either directly or through other kind of agencies such as Treasury for the sort of program assurance side of things, do you kind of foresee any capability issues with the commission delving into those areas?

Or do you feel as though you're adequately resourced and understand what's required in that space? Well, what I would say is that currently, the first task for this actually is getting in place a budget bid for it. So we're not currently funded to do this, and we need to put forward a business case with adequate funding to do that.

So the first part of your question is sort of, no, we need to get to the start line on the funding and resourcing side of things. It is a new function for central government. There are other asset owners around New Zealand that do this as a matter of course, and we have looked to them and their processes in trying to understand what the resourcing looks like. But the magnitude of the task is quite significant here, right? Because central government holds about 40% of all assets in New Zealand. And so, there's quite a bit of work to

understand what this looks like and rightsize it over time as well. I would also sort of bring in here, we've got Andy Hagen, who's the GM of investment, who's running this program. Andy, is there anything you would like to add to that?

Thanks, Jeff. Before I ask, can I just check that the sound's okay for the committee? Yeah. Your way it is. Whether it is when Jeff speaks again, we'll see. But anyway, thanks. We'll go back on mute when we- Thanks. I think to the member's question around capability, it's something that we are thinking very carefully about. The commission's put quite a lot of effort into, along with our colleagues across government, the treasury and the like, improving, and bringing a focus to asset management over the last year.

And so, for example, we invested heavily in putting together some guidance for agencies on asset management investment planning practices. Obviously, as part of that, we needed to build our own capability, to understand what good looks like and how that should play out in agency land. But as Jeff's alluded to, we do think that there's a build process to go.

As part of the budget bid that Jeff's alluded to, we're thinking about options for assurance, what that might look like. There are, of course, all sorts of options around depth, expectations, frequency. So we need to work through those things. That obviously has flow-on applications for the resourcing expertise that we need in-house.

Okay. Just one more. One more. Okay. I'll go to Simon and then Carlos. You've talked about central government. Local government obviously have quite a role when it comes to infrastructure around the country. What are the sort of next steps in terms of engagement with that sector?

Yeah. Well, what I would say is that one of the work programs we have moving forward is to take our forward guidance, which we have for different asset classes, but has been done more at a national level, and start to provide that more at a local level. And we have always tried to draw a connection between the work of forward guidance, signaling what we would expect to be spending in different sectors and different regions, and start connecting that with spatial planning, as it's imagined in the new resource management reform work.

And, so I think that that's a really important part of that in order to lock down what is likely to be a fundable program of capital infrastructure at the local level, rather than ending up in a similar place where we've been in the past with projects that are ultimately affordable. So I think that that's a really important part of the direction for local government. I think the other sort of issue that I would flag that we have had a lot of interactions with local government on is just the sustainability of infrastructure investment, particularly with respect to growth

patterns in New Zealand. And, we've made this point to the committee before, that we are growing in ways that is ultimately making the financials much more difficult for local government. And the significant challenge before us is to start moving the ship on that one and growing in a way that's making local governments financially stronger rather than financially weaker.

And that remains an issue that we think is really important to solve if we're going to crack the infrastructure issue. Actually, just on that, we've got Graeme Campbell, who's the Director of Economics and Research at the commission, who's running both of these programs. So I might just pause and see if there's anything he wants to add to that.

This is Graeme Campbell, Director of Economics and Research at the commission. I'm sorry, we broke up there at the beginning, so we didn't quite hear the question, although, I guess I'd say that Jeff's right, that we have a forward work program to develop forward guidance at more at a regional level to help inform long-run infrastructure planning and also a research agenda that includes further work in understanding how we can improve financial sustainability for infrastructure at the local level.

So yeah, these are two issues that are on our agenda. The other thing that I would just throw in there, of course, is the national infrastructure pipeline as well, where we now have pretty good representation from local government on their capital intentions plans. And for that work program, we want to get into a point where we're able to increasingly reflect back good insights to local government so that they can see how their plans look against other plans and help them use to sort of benchmark and right-size those plans as well. So we see that as a significant tool that can be used in this

space also. Thank you. Okay, thanks. Simon. Thank you. Good morning to the commission. Just looking at your Making Every Dollar Count report, which is heartening to hear that you're looking into this. I see in, and I'm looking at page 42, over a quarter of written assessment feedback cited the lack of low-cost options being considered. Insufficient consideration of lower cost or non-built solutions to infrastructure may be contributing to general cost growth over time.

What measures do you think the government should be considering to make sure that the lowest cost and non-built solutions are considered first, before additional scope or nice-to-haves are added? Yeah. There's a couple of things in here. First, I would say the investment decision hierarchy is really important, and various agencies have this kind of decision-making hierarchy, which starts with managing your existing assets, utilization of those assets, demand management, really asking the question: Do we need to build? And so I think that there's a part of this which is

about governance. There's a part of this which is about institutional culture sometimes. But I think simply asking these questions, what are the non-build options that we have in front of us here, is really useful. What we sort of talk to in that report is that as we've gone through and looked at a lot of the projects that have come to us, we're looking specifically excuse me, at the long-listing process down to the short-listing process.

And one of the metrics that we are looking at, usually that's done through a multi-criteria analysis, right? And how that process works is that a judgment will be made on what sort of allocation out of 100% is given to various attributes of the project. And one of the observations we've made is that cost is almost always less than 50%. Now, when a project is put forward in a cost-benefit analysis, that is by definition 50%. You're dividing one over the other.

So what we sort of see here, the inference here, is that in the long-listing process, we're using a methodology that is almost biasing itself towards the higher cost options, and then we're using a methodology that more routinely, or more appropriately, factors in cost. And we're ending up with really expensive options at the back end.

And that is a comment we would make not of any one sector, but of a general practice that we're seeing across infrastructure projects. Thank you. Thank you, Jeff. There's lots of supplementary coming, just bear any answer you've got here. But, Carlos. Thank you. The commission report actually outline a suitable potential approach to funding New Zealand future infrastructure needs.

How critical and scalable do you consider this funding mechanism to be in practice, particularly given that the difference in political views or people expectation or the skills of investment required and the long-term nature of the major infrastructure projects? Sorry, I missed the very first part of your question.

Were you talking about- Yes... a particular funding model? No, we're just saying that in your report, the commission report, the National Infrastructure Plan, you have mentioned that there's a suitable way to fund infrastructure, including PPP, user- Yeah... user pay for work- Right... or funding from overseas. I just want to know that all this different kind of funding mechanism, is it critical?

Or are we just trying to mention it for the sake of mentioning it in the report? Yes. So one sort of minor correction there. The PPP stuff and the sort of private capital, we would classify as a financing mechanism, not as a funding tool, right? Yes. Funding tools, ultimately, we are thinking about taxpayers, ratepayers, and users.

Investment funds are not going to fund New Zealand's infrastructure. We have to do that our ourselves. Yes Now, the plan really, I think one of the key observations of the plan is that networked infrastructure should be able to sort of fund itself off the network, and that it takes a sort of network users approach to paying for infrastructure.

And the rationale for that is so that we can free up capital for assets that are unable to do that because they don't necessarily have users, or there's just a very narrow path to doing that. And I'm thinking about things like schools and hospitals, and the defense estate, and so on and so forth.

We are in a world where that delineation between those two things has very much cracked, and we are starting to use consolidated revenues to fund networked utilities, particularly in land transport, and so we're getting pressures on the social infrastructure side. So the plan says as point one, to delineate between those and get back to a funding mechanism, particularly in land transport, that has the pricing tension within the network. That would be sort of point one.

Point two is, it really is talking more about why it's so important for users to see the price of the service that they are using. And this also is very important, right? Because it allows asset owners to understand where they should be investing, right?

For instance, if a gate charge is really high at an airport, this is a signal and a coordinating mechanism between the airline and the airport to consider putting in another gate. If you don't have that pricing signal, and you don't have the gate charge, and you fund it through a consolidated revenue, all of a sudden the asset owner is in a position of having to really guess more at where the additional capacity is needed. And we see sectors that are trying to do this through consolidated revenues have a really tough time because they're simply not

getting good pricing information about where the demand is. So as a result, I think the way that we price infrastructure is really material to the problems that we perceive are out there. And if we tend to reduce the user charge down to zero, as we do in, say, water or land transport at times, then what we'll end up having is overdemand, and we'll think we need to build more infrastructure.

But in fact, it's because we're not managing the demand effectively, and it gets into a bit of a cycle. Yeah. Callis. Can I just use a potential second harbor crossing as an example? I was going to... What was the funding model or combination of funding model do you think would be the most realistic for delivering a project of this size?

Well, the question that the commission asked at the outset of the work in the National Infrastructure Plan was looking at how difficult this project is to fund because of its size, right? And because of its size, it means that we're often having to look at either non-users within the network, which you're going to run into equity issues on, or non-users from outside the network, which the equity issues will be even harder. And so the question we asked is, well, given the capacity and resilience issues of the need for a new investment,

how much would the users of that investment be prepared to pay given the reduction in travel time and so on? And this is sort of known as the revenue maximizing toll for a new bridge, right? And the number that we had in the National Infrastructure Plan was a $9 toll that would get you a number of somewhere between $7 and $9 billion, as a beginning scope for what a sort of size of the project would look like, such that your users would use it for the benefits that it provides.

So what we were trying to do there is sort of reflect what a user perspective of project scope might look like. The moment you go outside of that number, you need to think about either asking non-users to pay, or as I say, folks from outside the network, right?

And there are various ways that you could do that. You can think about injections from consolidated revenue. You can think about IFF, and so on and so forth. But what stands as the issue to me is once you start doing that, you're getting into a world of crowding out a lot of other needs that will also be in front of you. And I think that that stands as one of the critical points to getting this project across the line.

Yes, this is what the- Sorry, what I'm going to do. I'm going to take Callis on this one, actually. I think there's a few steps around this because I'm really interested in this issue of funding for that network infrastructure, because there's been a few comments being made recently, but that fly right in the face of that. Oh, yeah. That was my question. Yeah. And this is why my supplementary go back to my primary question.

Like when you talk about now the user need to pay for it, or people nowadays expect everything for free, how can we change people mindset or expectation in order to implement or process the project? How can you do that? How do you change the mindset?

Yes, and people culture expectation. Yeah. I mean, it is kind of interesting to me that the number we came up with, particularly for this new crossing, was actually very similar, ballpark the same as the inflation adjusted number from the toll that was originally put across the harbor crossing when it started.

That is a sort of coincidence, and a lot of the media actually confused those two things, but it happened to be that the number was the same. I think part of this is a piece of advice that actually my old professor told me in the world of infrastructure, is that once you've got a toll in place, don't get rid of it. Don't get rid of it.

Because getting rid of a toll and then bringing it back is a very painful thing. And there is the sense that we should get rid of the tolls once the debt is paid back on the original capital project. But of course, it has to get through a renewal cycle.

Capital projects depreciate. And so in the first instance, the toll might serve as the way of paying back the debt on the loan, but in the long run, the toll is essential to find your way through a renewal cycle. Now, because we got rid of that toll many years ago, we're in a position where we're struggling to get through a renewal cycle, and people feel like the bridge is already paid for.

This is not what has happened with something like the Lower Thames Crossing, where they too are trying to get through a renewal cycle, but they kept the toll, right? And that has created the funding stream to see them through. Part of this story is helping communities understand that their assets depreciate, and they have to be renewed.

It is not just about funding the new capital expenditure. And that is why we have talked so much about the need to fund 60 cents on the dollar for renewals. It's not a small number. It's an enormous number. It gets bigger as a country matures.

And actually, I think like the infrastructure conversation has matured along these lines in the last couple of years, knowing what it takes to get through a renewal cycle. So I know there's a lot of fanfare about the new shiny project, but actually a big chunk of this is about how to get through a renewal cycle on the existing bridge.

Thank you. Tracy, are you in the same space? And Julianne, are you in the same space? I think if we could deal with this particular issue around, a lot of it's around transport funding renewals. And then Julianne, if you've got some other questions, we'll go to those as well. I've got some of this here too. So Tracy. Just a really quick add-on to that. In terms of what sort of thoughts or mechanisms I'm thinking about how do we stop that model disadvantaging small population places where the nationally significant infrastructure like South Island Freight, like what

tools, what mechanisms are within this to- accountability. Yeah. Well, as a general comment, I guess I would say that there is more infrastructure in large places, right? Infrastructure benefits from economies of scale. That's why when you drive into Auckland CBD, you're going to see a concentration of infrastructure. So clearly, as you sort of dissipate further away from the number of funders you have, the options, and what you can do, are necessarily impacted. One part of this is sound cost management, and is understanding what you would need to see to believe that a project could

stack up in an area with not as many people. In other words, what would be the sort of triggers you would be looking for? At what size of a population could we think about new water storage or another lane or another XXX? And I would look at that from the perspective of enough people to fund the operating and maintenance costs on the project, the interest payments on the debt, and then inevitably the renewal cycle.

With freight in particular, one of the challenge-- And I'll pass over to Graham. I might just pause and wait, hand this one over to Graham in a second as well. But one of the sort of interesting parts of freight networks is that they're using oftentimes the same infrastructure that we're using for personal travel, right? Like roads. And so they become a part of the demand stack of a road.

New Zealand is of a small enough nature and of a very elongated nature that the case for sort of separating out freight from passenger, in many places in New Zealand, we just need to be a lot bigger before we could fund ourselves through a renewal cycle on that quantum of infrastructure.

And that means oftentimes there's a sort of intermingling between these different parts of the demand stack for freight. But if you were to try and invest too much on one side or the other, you're going to end up in the same world that we've talked about for many other sectors, which is high capital stocks and not enough funders.

And then you're going to talk about maintenance issues, renewal problems. When we have our natural hazard events, are we going to be able to build back and so on? I'll just pause there because I know Graham Campbell also has been working in this space as well. I don't know if there's anything you would like to add to that, Graham. Yes, Jeff. Just a short bit to add for that.

When we've been looking at thinking long term about the financial sustainability of infrastructure, particularly in places where populations might not be able to support it completely on itself, the recommendation in the National Infrastructure Plan around for recommendation two for transport doesn't necessarily speak to every piece of every kilometer of the road network or the transport network needs to pay for itself. As Jeff mentioned, a couple of years ago, we put out a report which looked at strong pricing principles across network infrastructure.

The first one of those was setting pricing so that you can recover costs, which is what Jeff's been talking about. But another one of those important principles is having a pricing scheme that where there are benefits to reaching scale on the network, you might consider tweaks to your pricing methodology. And what we observe across some other infrastructure networks, for example, in electricity distribution transmission, is that not every bit of the network is paying for each individual piece.

But because there are benefits to everybody being on the network at the same time, some smaller population areas benefit from a sort of a cross-subsidy across the network because there is that benefit of scale. And so when we're thinking about good, strong pricing principles that can lead to quality infrastructure in those areas, which may not be able to support them on their own, I think Jeff's got the right idea here that the question we would be asking is, to what extent are there benefits of scale to the network as a whole to justify sort of a different pricing approach for

that? And I think for a lot of our land transport network, that is kind of the case where in areas which have lower population, we have built out a little bit more developed transport network for the areas such as freight because there are network benefits and benefits of scale. Julian, did you have a question specifically in this area?

And then I'll have a couple more- Yeah, actually, my question is pretty specifically in this area, and thanks very much. Jeff, you mentioned that land transport, as a network, ideally like water, you would be covering the cost of maintaining, renewing, and enhancing by user charges.

I'm just wondering, you've made the point on page eight of the plan that land transport funding system is unsustainable. It's been receiving a huge amount of Crown loans and grants that could have gone to other priority areas. Is continuing to freeze fuel excise duty where it is and borrow to cover the costs of the National Land Transport Fund in line with the commission's recommendations and the National Infrastructure Plan, or is it going in the opposite direction?

We would, of course, be looking at this over a longer time period, right, over a 30-year time period. And we have noted in the plan and other work as well that there is a significant gap between funding availability and capital investment intentions.

If it is the case that the-- And actually, I suppose one thing that I would add to this, looking back over the last sort of 30 years of fuel excise duty, it is true, of course, that we are down a lot from the peak. Over a 30-year period, though, we are on average up about 12%, right?

And so there is always going to be what I would describe- Sorry, Jeff. Jeff, can you be clear, up 12% on what? On the average over the last 30 years in inflation-adjusted terms, right? So we're way down if you just look over the last seven years, but if you look over the last 30 years, we're not doing too badly.

The point I would sort of make in here is that there is always pricing tension somewhere with an asset owner and a user. And our job really is to assess, I think, where a reasonable place to land on a price is likely to be such that you don't have contestability pushing it back down the other way.

And of course, this is determined by the value of the projects. If people are seeing that projects are reducing their travel times by several hours, you could expect prices to go up as a result, so they're happy to fund those projects. But as the project quality narrows, you might actually start to see more pricing tension come into it. With the forward guidance, I think you can back out numbers associated with fuel excise duty, and Graham, correct me if I'm wrong, but I think that those are somewhere within the realm of five cents up to a little over twenty cents, I think is the

number over a 30-year period. So it's not nothing, and we're baking in an increase in prices there. But ultimately, what the plan is saying is that land transport and demand for land transport are under increasing pressure from a few things.

Changing demographics, we are getting older, and older people use transport networks less, right? We're moving from a world of 5% annual average growth rates several decades ago on our roading networks to numbers that are much closer to zero to 1%, right? So there is quite a change in the profile of demand.

At the same time, what we're seeing is a real shift from new capital investment to maintenance and renewals, partly because that growth is slowing, and also I should say income growth as well, which is a driver. So we're sort of shifting more towards that.

But of course, the other thing in here is natural hazards, which essentially means that our depreciation rates on a lot of our assets are higher, look like they're probably going to be higher in the future than what they have been in the past. And so that is going to start shifting more from new capital to maintenance and renewals in the longer term.

So Graham, I don't know if you want to comment specifically on the pricing assumptions and the forward guidance over the longer term. Yeah, just briefly, what I'd say is that, just to echo what Jeff said, the forecast and the forward guidance for land transport does take a longer-term view.

And you'll note in the forward guidance for land transport, the percentage of UDP that we would sort of see as the affordable and sustainable level is lower than what we have been spending over the last 20 years. And so in some ways, the pricing tension that we're seeing right now, sort of the desire to keep fuel excise duties and road user charges flat or keep them where they are, is we think sort of a manifestation of what we've sort of forecasted at a macro level.

Those slower population growth, slower income growth, demand or vehicle kilometer travel growth slowing down a bit. And so I guess we would sort of see this as a natural response to what the dynamics and the forward guidance have. The numbers that Jeff cited around what we would-- If you take the forward guidance and you try to translate those to fuel excise duty and road user charges, the forward guidance does not assume that fuel excise duties and road user charges will be flat over the next 30 years, for two reasons.

One, the forward guidance is a long-term forecast, so it's very possible that over windows of time, you would have investment below or above that, which would require higher or lower fuel excise duties and road user charges. And the second is those revenues fund not just capital expenditure, but they also fund a lot of operational expenditure, so road safety, maintenance of the road. So that's not CapEx per se.

We're talking sweeping things off the road. But also public transport services are paid for by those revenue sources. So our analysis needed to make sort of assumptions about that. But the thrust of it is that the forward guidance doesn't assume flat road user charges. And a big chunk of the reason that is, is because even though we have those headwinds from population growth and income growth slowing, just generally construction prices tend to rise faster than the overall economy's prices. And so, in order to sort of fund the investment that we think people will

demand, you will have to increase charges over time. So- But just speaking to this recommendation about the system returning to a model where the cost of maintaining, renewing, and enhancing the existing network is predominantly met by users. If in the next three years or the next year or two, governments are deciding, and parties in Parliament are deciding to continue to increase the amount of general Crown funding that's going in to pay for the land transport system, is that in line with the overall direction of returning to user

charges, or is it going in the opposite direction? I would say, yeah, you're quite right. The plan has said that a high-performing land transport network is one that has a ring-fenced model of funding. That is very much part and parcel of recommendation two.

If it's the case that FED is being kept lower and capital intentions remain the same, then yes, it would push in that direction. If there is a change to capital intentions that is commensurate to the reduction, then it might go the other way. But- So it's really the, whether or not Crown funding, general Crown revenue is being used to pay for the land transport system or if, okay, maybe we're not increasing revenue from users, but we're reducing spending in line with that, then that's more in the direction of what you're recommending in the

National Infrastructure Plan. I'd say that's a really good characterization. Yeah. So can I just check, Jeff, you said 12%, so over the past 30 odd years, because there was a stage where we had, before we got to the full hypothecation, where in fact money was being taken from FED and RAC and being used for the General Consolidated Fund. So the impression I've got is that in fact, transport was paying for other stuff. Now we've reversed it and the Crown is paying for transport things. But you're saying over the 30 years, if I understood you right, the 30

years passed, that we've had transport at least paying for itself. But looking forward, that may well not be the case. Well, it clearly isn't at the moment. Yeah, it certainly hasn't been the last few years, and I think it's not projected to be for the next few years as well. So, but yeah, I'm certainly happy to send you the work that we've done looking at how these prices have changed over the last 30 years, which has motivated- So this goes-- I'd be really interested in that because, I mean, obviously the issue that Julianne has raised, one I was going to raise as well, which we've had

political parties sort of saying, well, we want the Crown to fund the gap in transport funding for the next year or the next three years, depending on which party it is. That does seem slightly antithetical to the direction that you're encouraging us to take. But what you said earlier also was the tripling in cost of delivery. Be really interested to hear a little bit more about that.

And we had a meeting with civil contractors the other day, and they said that, because we talk about productivity, and they said that what we're now measuring, they thought it was a pretty rough measure, rough reading measure, which is basically how many kilometers did you deliver for how much money. So the work that we put out yesterday essentially tries to boil this down into three areas, right? We're looking at input prices, we're looking at productivity, which is how we convert those inputs into services, and then we're looking at questions of scope on the project.

So with input prices, we're thinking about things like wages, labor. We're thinking about concrete, structural steel, timber. These are the sort of main inputs for infrastructure projects. And we're looking at how our prices are benchmarked against the range of other countries.

And the good news there is that we are essentially, with the exception of some things that have to be sourced locally, like aggregates, we are essentially buying in international prices, and we look more or less aligned on a lot of those things. When we look at the kind of drivers of scope, they are numerous and they are many, right? There's a sort of consenting story to this.

There is a community expectation story. But what I would say is that when it comes to public infrastructure, the ability to confine scope is very, very challenging. And we typically meet questions of, "Well, can we have this or can we have that?" with bigger scope and bigger scope and bigger scope.

And that's fine, but at the end of the day, the question that we're asking is: How does that impact on willingness to pay across all of the services that we need? So we're essentially saying that it looks like of all of the rocks that you want to turn over to understand why these costs are really increasing, questions of scope loom large. And in the sectors that have strong regulation, regulatory oversight, asking questions about, "Is the consumer willing to pay for this asset, for the operation, maintenance, and renewal of this asset into the future?" you tend to see stronger control on scope.
